intro:
The dramatic historical catalyst of Sūrah al-Mumtaḥanah occurred in Ramaḍān of 8 AH (630 CE), as the Prophet ﷺ was secretly preparing a massive army of ten thousand men for the historic conquest and liberation of Makkah, following the Quraysh's breach of the Treaty of Ḥudaybiyah. Divinely informed of the treason, the Prophet dispatched ʿAlī, al-Zubayr, and al-Miqdād, who intercepted the woman at the garden of Khākh, extracted the parchment from her hair, and brought it back to Madinah. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb drew his sword in fury, shouting: *“O Messenger of Allah, let me strike the neck of this hypocrite!”* The Prophet turned gently to Ḥāṭib, who wept and confessed: *“Do not be in haste with me, O Messenger of Allah! I have not disbelieved or apostatized; I only wished to establish a favor with the Quraysh so they might protect my family.”* The Prophet ﷺ turned to ʿUmar and said: *“He has spoken the truth. What do you know, O ʿUmar? Perhaps Allah looked upon the veterans of Badr and declared: 'Do whatever you will, for I have already forgiven you!'”* Verses 1–3 descended immediately: reprimanding the believers for extending clandestine affection to enemies actively waging war against them, but initiating a profound, nuanced legal framework for international relations.

**The Structural Modulation and the Golden Rule of Foreign Policy**

The architecture of Sūrah al-Mumtaḥanah is structured across three distinct movements:

1. The Reprimand of Compromised Loyalty and the Abrahamic pattern (1–6): Opens with the uncompromising command: *“O you who have believed, do not take My enemies and your enemies as allies, extending an offer of friendship to them while they have disbelieved in what came to you of the truth, having driven out the Messenger and yourselves [simply] because you believe in Allah, your Lord”* (60:1). It sets forward Abraham and his companions as the supreme, excellent model (*uswatun ḥasanah*): declaring to their idolatrous people their total disassociation from injustice until they believe in Allah alone, while recording Abraham's exceptional promise of forgiveness for his father as an exception that must not be imitated.

2. The Golden Rule of Peace and Engagement (7–9): Delivering a ray of prophetic hope: *“Perhaps Allah will put, between you and those to whom you have been enemies among them, affection. And Allah is competent, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful”* (60:7)—a prophecy fulfilled when Makkah embraced Islam months later. Verses 8–9 establish the eternal, foundational charter of Islamic international relations: - *Positive Engagement*: *“Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you because of religion and do not expel you from your homes—from being righteous toward them and acting justly toward them. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly (*al-muqsiṭīn*)”* (60:8). - *Hostile Non-Alliance*: *“Allah only forbids you from those who fight you because of religion and expel you from your homes and aid in your expulsion—[forbids] that you make allies of them. And whoever makes allies of them, then it is those who are the wrongdoers”* (60:9).

3. The Examination of Women and the Pledge of Allegiance (10–13): Regulating the refugee status of believing women fleeing Makkah, establishing that they cannot be returned to pagan husbands, returning their dowries to maintain economic fairness. Codifying the celebrated *Women's Pledge of Allegiance* (*Bayʿat al-Nisāʾ*, 60:12 — *“O Prophet! When the believing women come to you, pledging to you that they will neither associate anything with Allah ˹in worship˺, nor steal, nor fornicate, nor kill their children, nor falsely attribute ˹illegitimate˺ children to their husbands, nor disobey you in what is right, then accept their pledge, and ask Allah to forgive them.”*) directly to the Prophet ﷺ: pledging not to associate partners with God, not to steal, not to commit adultery, not to kill their children, not to produce slander fabricated between their hands and feet, and not to disobey the Prophet in that which is good. The sūrah concludes by reiterating the prohibition of allying with those who have incurred the wrath of God and despaired of the Hereafter.

verses.1:
> O believers! Do not take My enemies and yours as trusted allies, showing them affection even though they deny what has come to you of the truth. They drove the Messenger and yourselves out ˹of Mecca˺, simply for your belief in Allah, your Lord. If you ˹truly˺ emigrated to struggle in My cause and seek My pleasure, ˹then do not take them as allies,˺ disclosing secrets ˹of the believers˺ to the pagans out of affection for them, when I know best whatever you conceal and whatever you reveal. And whoever of you does this has truly strayed from the Right Way

**Alliance Is a Bond, Not a Mood**

The noun the verse forbids is *awliyāʾ*, the plural of *walī*: the person who has charge of your affair, the patron whose support you lean on when you cannot stand alone. What made the act plausible was *mawadda*, the warm affection the believers still carried for their own people in Mecca — parents, cousins, the companions of childhood. It reserves its strongest language for the love owed to God: “Still there are some who take others as Allah’s equal—they love them as they should love Allah—but the ˹true˺ believers love Allah even more.” (2:165). A believer may feel tenderness for a relative who rejects the message; he may not hand that relative the place that belongs to God and His Messenger, which is what *walī* means in practice.

**The Letter Carried Out of Madinah**

This verse was revealed in the run-up to the march on Mecca in 8/630, and the incident behind it survives in detail. Ḥāṭib ibn Abī Baltaʿah, an Emigrant who had fought at Badr, wrote to leading men of Quraysh to warn them that the Prophet was preparing to come against them. The Prophet sent ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib with al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām and al-Miqdād ibn al-Aswad, telling them that a woman travelling at Rawḍat Khākh carried a letter. They found her, and when she denied having anything, she brought it out of her braid (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3007). The document would have cost the Muslims the advantage of surprise against a city that still held their confiscated homes and their estranged kin. To call this a lapse of courtesy would be generous. The verse’s own description is *disclosing secrets ˹of the believers˺ to the pagans* (60:1 — *“O believers! Do not take My enemies and yours as trusted allies, showing them affection even though they deny what has come to you of the truth.”*) — intelligence handed to a party that had already driven the Messenger and his community out of Mecca, and the disclosure of a military plan is not a private matter between friends.

**What Ḥāṭib Said in His Defence**

Ibn Kathir adds some background that explains why Ḥāṭib did it. Ḥāṭib was one of the early Emigrants, but he was not of Quraysh by birth. He lived among them as an ally, and he had left children and property behind in Makkah. When the Prophet decided to march on the city after its people broke the treaty, he told the Muslims to get ready and prayed, “O Allah, keep our news hidden from them.” The letter was a direct threat to that prayer. Ibn Kathir notes that God told His Messenger about the letter because He had accepted the prayer to keep the news hidden.

In the version Imam Aḥmad recorded from ʿAlī, the Prophet asked, “O Ḥāṭib, what is this?” Ḥāṭib answered: “O Messenger of Allah, do not be hasty with me. I was a man attached to Quraysh, not one of them. The other Emigrants with you have relatives in Makkah who protect their families. I have no blood ties there, so I wanted to do them a favour so that they would protect my relatives. I did not do it out of disbelief, or to leave my religion, or because I prefer disbelief after Islam.” The Prophet told his Companions, “He has told you the truth.” So the Prophet judged Ḥāṭib by the reason Ḥāṭib gave and by his record at Badr. He did not judge him by how bad the act looked. This matches the sūrah’s own language: it scolds the believers for the act but still calls them *believers*.

**Whether the Verse Was Named in the Report**

Ibn Kathir says that all the major collections except Ibn Mājah have this ḥadīth, through chains that include Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah. He then records a careful point about how it was passed on. Al-Bukhārī placed the report in his chapter on the Prophet’s campaigns and added that God then revealed the sūrah. But in another place in his Ṣaḥīḥ he notes that ʿAmr, one of the narrators, said the verse was revealed about Ḥāṭib, yet he did not know whether the mention of the verse was part of the ḥadīth itself or a narrator’s explanation. When Sufyān was asked about it, he said, “This is the narration I took from ʿAmr. I did not leave out a letter of it. I do not know whether anyone else memorised the same words.” The link between the letter and the verse is therefore firm, and early narrators were careful to separate what they had heard from what they understood.

**The Same Boundary Drawn Elsewhere**

The prohibition is not unique to the opening of this sūrah, and its repetitions show what pressure each version answers. “O believers! Do not take your parents and siblings as trusted allies if they choose disbelief over belief.” (9:23) names the family. “O believers! Do not take disbelievers as allies instead of the believers.” (4:144) names the community. The sharpest form names the whole social world: “You will never find a people who ˹truly˺ believe in Allah and the Last Day loyal to those who defy Allah and His Messenger, even if they were their parents, children, siblings, or extended family.” (58:22). Read together, the verses trace a boundary of allegiance rather than a policy of hostility toward outsiders as such, and the sūrah itself goes on to distinguish the two categories with care.

**Their Only Charge Was Faith**

The verse gives the reason for the expulsion in one short phrase: *simply for your belief in Allah, your Lord*. Ibn Kathir explains it as if God were saying, “Your only fault in their eyes was that you believed in Allah, the Lord of all that exists.” The Book uses the same bitter irony for the believers of the ditch, who were persecuted (85:8 — *“who they resented for no reason other than belief in Allah—the Almighty, the Praiseworthy—”*), and for the Emigrants themselves (22:40 — *“˹They are˺ those who have been expelled from their homes for no reason other than proclaiming: “Our Lord is Allah.”*). The point matters for the ruling. The enemies named here are not people who happen to disagree with the believers. They drove the believers out of their homes because of their faith. The friendship is forbidden because of that hostility, not because of a difference in belief alone.

The next clause, *if you ˹truly˺ emigrated to struggle in My cause and seek My pleasure*, is a condition, and Ibn Kathir spells out what it means: if that is really why you left, then do not take My enemies and yours as allies after they have driven you from your homes and property out of anger at you and rejection of your religion. The Emigrant’s own journey is used as the argument. A man who gave up his home for God’s pleasure cannot spend what is left of that home buying protection from the people who took it.

**The Occasion of Revelation**

The verse came down over Ḥāṭib ibn Abī Baltaʿah, a man of the community who had fought at Badr. When the Prophet prepared to march for Makkah, Ḥāṭib wrote to the men of that city warning them of the approach and sent the letter with a woman, and the news reached the Prophet through the revelation. ʿUmar asked to be allowed to strike his neck, and the Prophet refused, saying that the man had been present at Badr and that God had said of the men of Badr that they may do as they please. The report is in Bukhārī and Muslim, and the verse in front of us is read as the answer to that letter.

**What the Men of Makkah Had Done**

The verse lists their offences so that the community would not treat the friendship as an even exchange. They had driven the Prophet and the believers out, denied the truth when it came, and tried to take back the man who had put his trust in God. The Book mentions the expulsion in several places, and it commands the believers in the same sūrah to deal kindly and justly with those who had not fought them or driven them out (60:8 — *“Allah does not forbid you from dealing kindly and fairly with those who have neither fought nor driven you out of your homes. Surely Allah loves those who are fair”*). The two verses are read together for that reason: the prohibition belongs to those who were at war with the community, and the Book is careful to say which group that is.

**The Command and the Word for Loyalty**

The verb the verse forbids is taking these people as *awliyāʾ*, which covers support, patronage and confidential reliance. The Book uses the same word in the Sūrah of the Table when it forbids taking the men of the two earlier communities as patrons over the believers (5:51 — *“O believers! Take neither Jews nor Christians as guardians—they are guardians of each other. Whoever does so will be counted as one of them. Surely Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people”*; 5:57 — *“O believers! Do not seek the guardianship of those given the Scripture before you and the disbelievers who have made your faith a mockery and amusement. And be mindful of Allah if you are ˹truly˺ believers”*), and the Sūrah of the Women states the same rule when the community is under pressure (4:139 — *“who choose disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. Do they seek honour and power through that company? Surely all honour and power belongs to Allah”*). The passage then gives the example of Abraham, who cut off his father when the man persisted in hostility (60:4 — *“The only exception is when Abraham said to his father, “I will seek forgiveness for you,˹” adding, “but˺ I cannot protect you from Allah at all.”*), and it ends by holding out the hope that God may yet put friendship between the two groups, since God is able (60:7 — *“˹In time,˺ Allah may bring about goodwill between you and those of them you ˹now˺ hold as enemies. For Allah is Most Capable. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”*). The command is about the war, and the sūrah says so in the same breath.

**The Exception for Real Danger**

Ibn Kathir sets this verse beside the other places where the Book forbids alliance with disbelievers, and one of them contains a small exception. The prohibition in Sūrah Āl ʿImrān carries a clause for self-protection (3:28 — *“Believers should not take disbelievers as guardians instead of the believers—and whoever does so will have nothing to hope for from Allah—unless it is a precaution against their tyranny.”*). He links that exception directly to Ḥāṭib. He says this is why the Prophet accepted Ḥāṭib’s excuse that he had only wanted a favour from Quraysh for the sake of the family and property he had left behind in Makkah. The excuse did not make the letter right. It did explain why a man who acted out of fear for his family was not treated as one who had changed sides. For the reader, the two cases stay separate. A defensive step taken under real threat is judged differently from loyalty given freely to the enemy.
verses.2:
> If they gain the upper hand over you, they would be your ˹open˺ enemies, unleashing their hands and tongues to harm you, and wishing that you would abandon faith

**Hands First, and Then Tongues**

The two instruments of the hostility are named in order: hands stretched out in violence, then tongues stretched out in harm. Classical commentary takes the hands as fighting and killing, and the tongues as insult, mockery, and slander. In Sūrat al-Aḥzāb, the hypocrites who stayed behind and then returned to the safety of Madinah are described as slashing the believers with razor-sharp tongues once the danger has passed (33:19 — *“But once the danger is over, they slash you with razor-sharp tongues, ravenous for ˹worldly˺ gains.”*) — the same injury, delivered from a place of safety. Believers are told plainly that they will hear much hurtful speech from those given the Scripture before them and from the polytheists, and that patience is the answer to it (3:186 — *“You ˹believers˺ will surely be tested in your wealth and yourselves, and you will certainly hear many hurtful words from those who were given the Scripture before you and ˹from˺ the polytheists.”*).

**The Wish That Runs Beneath Both**

The sentence ends with desire: they wish you would abandon faith. The verb is *yawaddū*, from the same root as *mawadda*, the affection named in the preceding verse, and the echo is the point. Whatever warmth the believers were sending to Mecca, what came back was not neutral coexistence but a wish aimed at the heart of their religion. The Book records the same wish from the same quarter again and again. “Many among the People of the Book wish they could turn you ˹believers˺ back to disbelief because of their envy, after the truth has been made clear to them.” (2:109). And “Some of the People of the Book wish to mislead you ˹believers˺. They mislead none but themselves, yet they fail to perceive it.” (3:69). A wish of that kind turns every other relationship into an instrument. The friendship is real as far as the enemy is concerned, but its object is not the believer’s welfare; it is the believer’s reversal. That is why the verse can describe men as both affectionate and hostile in the same breath, and why the earlier prohibition was a matter of self-preservation rather than of pride.

Ibn Kathir reads the verse as God explaining the hostility in full: if they ever gain the upper hand, they will use every kind of harm they can, in word and in deed. And they wish that the believers would *disbelieve*, which he explains as a wish that the believers never gain anything good at all. Then he draws the conclusion the verse wants the reader to draw: “Their enmity to you is outward and inward, so how can you become supporters of this type of people?” He adds that the verse is meant to strengthen the believers’ resolve against them. The argument is built from their own conduct. It does not ask the believers to imagine what the enemy might do. It points to what the enemy has already done, and to what he says he wants.

**Reading Interests Instead of Manners**

Sūrah al-Mumtaḥanah teaches a hard lesson in judgement: courtesy is not evidence of intention. A community that mistakes good manners for good will is defenceless, because manners cost nothing while intentions are expensive. The criterion given here is conduct under pressure — what a party does when the upper hand is in its grip. At the same time the verse is not a licence for suspicion of every stranger, and the Book guards the other side of the balance: “Fight in the cause of Allah ˹only˺ against those who wage war against you, but do not exceed the limits.” (2:190). The hostility described is not a suspicion but a record: these are the people who deny what has come to you of the truth and who drove the Messenger and the believers from their homes (60:1 — *“They drove the Messenger and yourselves out ˹of Mecca˺, simply for your belief in Allah, your Lord.”*). Judgement rests on what is known, not on what is feared, and the sūrah will later mark the difference between enemies who fight and those who do not.

**The Same Warning in Sūrat al-Tawbah**

Sūrat al-Tawbah states the identical situation — enemies who are trusted while powerless and rapacious when strong. “If they were to have the upper hand over you, they would have no respect for kinship or treaty. They only flatter you with their tongues, but their hearts are in denial, and most of them are rebellious.” (9:8). That verse adds a detail this one implies: the flattery is itself the instrument, smooth speech covering a settled refusal. It also asks the question that follows from the revelation of al-Mumtaḥanah’s opening: “Will you not fight those who have broken their oaths, conspired to expel the Messenger ˹from Mecca˺, and attacked you first? Do you fear them?” (9:13). Two sūrahs, one diagnosis. The enemy is defined by his aim, not by his tone of voice, and the community that has been driven from its homes is told to see clearly rather than to pretend.
verses.3:
> Neither your relatives nor children will benefit you on Judgment Day—He will decide between you ˹all˺. For Allah is All-Seeing of what you do

**Two Ways to Attach the Day**

The sentence admits a second syntactic arrangement that the commentators record. One may read it as “Neither your relatives nor children will benefit you on Judgment Day—He will decide between you ˹all˺.” (60:3) so that the negation belongs to the whole clause of benefit: whatever the day, kin and children are not the currency. Or one may attach the time phrase to the first clause only — the relatives and children will not benefit you on that Day (60:3 — *“Neither your relatives nor children will benefit you on Judgment Day—He will decide between you ˹all˺. For Allah is All-Seeing of what you do”*) — leaving the separation between the two groups as an independent statement. The two readings differ in scope, not in doctrine. The first is the more sweeping and the more likely to have been intended, since the Book uses the same argument elsewhere without limiting it to a single day: “Wealth and children are the adornment of this worldly life. The everlasting good deeds are far better with your Lord in reward and in hope.” (18:46). The second keeps the verse tightly anchored to the resurrection scene that the sūrah has been building. Neither permits the reader to keep a lever that the verse has just removed.

**Every Soul Arrives Alone**

The Qur’an describes the resurrection as the collapse of genealogy into individuals. The trumpet is blown and there is no kinship between them on that Day, nor does anyone ask about another (23:101 — *“Then, when the Trumpet will be blown, there will be no kinship between them on that Day, nor will they ˹even care to˺ ask about one another”*) — the very thing that every tribe takes for granted, the mutual inquiry of relatives on the day of catastrophe, is gone. And the Book states the principle without qualification: “No soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another. Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you of what you used to do.” (39:7). This is why the sūrah’s teaching is not harshness. A community that thinks family can cover a defect will keep building on sand, and the single greatest mercy that can be granted to it is to be told, in advance, that the sand will not hold. The believer who is separated from his kin by their disbelief loses a bond in time; the verse argues that the bond was already on loan, and that only the faith he carries into that court will be his own possession.

**God Sees the Deed, Not the Lineage**

The verse seals the matter with a single attribute: “For Allah is All-Seeing of what you do.” (60:3). The object of the seeing is works — *ʿamal* — not ancestry, not the size of a family, not the eloquence of a claim. This closing formula is one the Book uses when it wants to place responsibility exactly where it belongs, and it recurs with the same function: “O believers! Stand firm for Allah and bear true testimony. Do not let the hatred of a people lead you to injustice. Be just! That is closer to righteousness. And be mindful of Allah. Surely Allah is All-Aware of what you do.” (5:8). Sūrat al-Mumtaḥanah opens with a man who acted out of family feeling and closes this early passage by removing family feeling from the scale of judgement. What remains on the scale is the deed. The believer is not asked to stop loving his kin; he is told that love will not testify for him, and that only his own record will be read aloud.

The Book repeats the point across many sūrahs in varied words: the Day when neither wealth nor children will be of any benefit (26:88 — *“the Day when neither wealth nor children will be of any benefit”*), the Day when no parent will be of any benefit to their child, nor a child to their parent (31:33 — *“O humanity! Be mindful of your Lord, and beware of a Day when no parent will be of any benefit to their child, nor will a child be of any benefit to their parent.”*).

**Kinship Even With a Prophet**

Ibn Kathir gives the plain meaning of the verse: your family ties will not help you with God if He has decided to punish you, and they will not help you if you please your relatives by doing what angers Him. Those who go along with their families’ disbelief to keep them happy have earned loss and failure, and their deeds are wasted. Then he adds a sentence that makes the verse sharper: the relationship will not help them with God even if it was with a prophet. The Book gives examples of this elsewhere, such as the son of Noah and the father of Abraham, whose story comes in the next verse.

To show this, Ibn Kathir cites a report that Imam Aḥmad recorded from Anas, which Muslim and Abū Dāwūd also collected. A man asked the Prophet, “O Messenger of Allah, where is my father?” He said, “In the Fire.” As the man turned away, the Prophet called him back and said, “My father and your father are in the Fire.” The second sentence was said out of kindness. It told the man that his grief was not a mark of lower rank, and that the Prophet himself stood under the same law. That is exactly the verse’s teaching. On the Day of Judgement no one is saved by whom they descend from. Only the deed counts, and it is weighed by the One who *is All-Seeing of what you do*.
verses.4:
> You already have an excellent example in Abraham and those with him, when they said to their people, “We totally dissociate ourselves from you and ˹shun˺ whatever ˹idols˺ you worship besides Allah. We reject you. The enmity and hatred that has arisen between us and you will last until you believe in Allah alone.” The only exception is when Abraham said to his father, “I will seek forgiveness for you,˹” adding, “but˺ I cannot protect you from Allah at all.” ˹The believers prayed,˺ “Our Lord! In You we trust. And to You we ˹always˺ turn. And to You is the final return

**What the Word “Example” Carries Here**

*Uswa* is not a lesson learned from a story; it is a pattern a person follows, the model whose condition you adopt and reproduce. The verse says that Abraham and those with him have been exactly that for the believers — *qad kānat lakum uswatun ḥasana* — and it places the model next to the hardest command the community had received, the cutting of loyalties to its own people. The Book uses the same phrase of the Prophet himself: “Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah you have an excellent example for whoever has hope in Allah and the Last Day, and remembers Allah often.” (33:21). Abraham is named as the pattern for the same work in a different age, which is the Qur’anic way of showing that the demand is not an innovation of Madinah.

**The Exception Made for a Father**

The verse then excludes one sentence from the model: Abraham’s promise to seek forgiveness for his father, with the admission attached to it that he had no power to avail him anything against Allah. The promise was real, and Abraham kept it for as long as it could be kept — the Book elsewhere records that his prayer was in fulfilment of a promise he had made, and that when it became clear to him his father was an enemy of Allah, he repudiated him (9:114 — *“As for Abraham’s prayer for his father’s forgiveness, it was only in fulfilment of a promise he had made to him.”*). So the exclusion is not a rebuke of a misconducted prayer; it is a statement that this particular act belongs to a stage of Abraham’s story that cannot be imitated as a rule. The commentators agree that a Muslim is not commanded to seek forgiveness for those who die in denial, since the request presumes a repentance that is not there. The verse teaches something sharper still by including the exception at all.

**Why the Exception Had to Be Spelled Out**

Ibn Kathir explains why the verse makes an exception for Abraham’s promise. Some of the believers had been praying for forgiveness for parents who died as polytheists, and they cited Abraham’s prayer for his father as their precedent. The Book answered them in Sūrat al-Tawbah (9:113 — *“It is not ˹proper˺ for the Prophet and the believers to seek forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were close relatives, after it has become clear to the believers that they are bound for the Hellfire”*), and in the next verse it explains that Abraham’s prayer was only to keep a promise, and that once it was clear his father was an enemy of God, he disowned him (9:114, quoted above). So the exception here means that you cannot use Abraham’s example to argue that it is allowed to seek forgiveness for those who died in shirk. Ibn Kathir says this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and several others.

He also explains the declaration itself, phrase by phrase. *We totally dissociate ourselves from you* means “we disown you”. *We reject you* means “we reject your religion and your way”. The enmity and hatred have appeared “from now, and for as long as you remain on your disbelief”. And *until you believe in Allah alone* means until they worship God alone without partners and give up the idols and rivals they worship besides Him. Read this way, the hostility has a clear end point. It is tied to the idolatry, and it ends when the idolatry ends. That is why the sūrah can later hope that God will turn enemies into friends (60:7) without going back on anything said here.

**A Prayer of Trust at the End**

The section closes with a prayer: “Our Lord! In You we trust. And to You we ˹always˺ turn. And to You is the final return.” (60:4). Three verbs, and each one answers a temptation in the situation. *Tawakkul*, entrusting one’s affairs to God, replaces the tribal protector that a man like Ḥāṭib wanted to secure. *Ināba*, turning back to God repeatedly, describes the lifelong motion of a creature who drifts and returns. *Maṣīr*, the journey’s end, reminds the one who prays that all roads, including the road of the Emigrants, finish at the same destination. The translation places these words in the mouths of the believers, and that reading makes good sense of the passage: the community that has just lost its earthly supports is taught what to say instead. This is the model in its practical form. Abraham left a city, and what he carried out of it was a trust that no city could take back, which is the whole lesson the sūrah wants a frightened community to learn.

The Book records the same declaration from Abraham in another sūrah with the same elements: “˹Remember, O Prophet˺ when Abraham declared to his father and his people, ‘I am totally free of whatever ˹gods˺ you worship, except the One Who originated me, and He will surely guide me.’” (43:26–27).

**What the Example Consists Of**

The verse presents Abraham and his companions as the pattern for the community, and it gives the first part of what they did: they told their people that they were free of them and of what they worship besides God, and that there was open enmity between them until the people believed in God alone. The verse then records that Abraham asked forgiveness for his father, and it explains that he had a promise to him in the matter (60:4 continues into the next verse — *“You already have an excellent example in Abraham and those with him”*). The Book gives the readers the model of a person who broke with his community without hatred, and the sentence about enmity is the one the community in Madinah most needed to hear.

**What the Commentators Explained**

The older commentators read the verse as the model for the men and women who had left Makkah, and they noted the two things the pattern contains: a clear separation in religion and an absence of personal vengeance. The Sūrah of the Night Journey states the same rule for the children of Israel's history, and the Book's command to speak to the men who are not fighting with kindness and justice (60:8 — *“Allah does not forbid you from dealing kindly and fairly with those who have neither fought nor driven you out of your homes. Surely Allah loves those who are fair”*) is placed a few verses after the example. The community's jurists read the two together whenever the question of dealing with the hostile part of a family was raised.

**Where the Passage Is Standing**

The sūrah was given after the treaty at Ḥudaybiyyah, and the men of the community had families on the other side of the line. The verse in front of us gives them Abraham and his companions, and the verses that follow give the hope that God may yet put affection between the two groups (60:7 — *“˹In time,˺ Allah may bring about goodwill between you and those of them you ˹now˺ hold as enemies. For Allah is Most Capable. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”*). The Book's arrangement keeps the model and the open door in the same passage.
verses.5:
> Our Lord! Do not subject us to the persecution of the disbelievers. Forgive us, our Lord! You ˹alone˺ are truly the Almighty, All-Wise.”

**Moses’ People Prayed the Same Way**

The prayer has a precedent in the Book in nearly these words. When the people of Moses lost their children to Pharaoh’s campaign of slaughter and were still without a state of their own, they said: “In Allah we trust. Our Lord! Do not subject us to the persecution of the oppressive people, and deliver us by Your mercy from the disbelieving people.” (10:85–86). The similarity is not accidental. Sūrat al-Mumtaḥanah belongs to a community in the same shape: believers without power in the very city that has expelled them, facing an enemy that could still reach their family members. The Book repeatedly gives such communities the same vocabulary instead of new answers, and the reuse is itself a form of instruction. What was asked in Egypt and what is asked in Madinah is what the weak have always needed: not merely safety, but safety that does not come at the cost of the truth they are carrying. The verse teaches the believers to ask for the version of relief in which God is still the one who is proven right.

**What the Early Commentators Heard in the Prayer**

The phrase translated *do not subject us to the persecution of the disbelievers* is literally “do not make us a *fitnah* for those who disbelieve”, and Ibn Kathir collects the early explanations of what that means. Mujāhid said: “Do not punish us at their hands, or with a punishment from You, so that they say, ‘If these people were following the truth, this would not have happened to them.’” Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said something similar. Qatādah said: “Do not give the disbelievers victory over us so that we are tried at their hands. If You did, they would think they had been given victory because they are right.” Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī preferred this meaning. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās: “Do not give them power over us, so that we suffer trials at their hands.” All these readings say the same thing. The believers are not only asking to be spared pain. They are asking that their suffering not be used as an argument against the truth they carry.

**Why a Believer’s Defeat Teaches a Lie**

The petition rests on a sober view of how people read history. A community that says God is with it and then disappears from the field has taught a lesson its enemies will absorb at once. The Qur’an speaks of the other side of this situation in Sūrat al-Burūj, where the persecutors of believing men and women who do not repent are promised the punishment of Hell and the torment of burning (85:10 — *“Those who persecute the believing men and women and then do not repent will certainly suffer the punishment of Hell and the torment of burning”*). Before that verse, the Book states the arrangement plainly: “We have made some of you a trial for others.” (25:20). The trial is structural. Believers are tested by opposition, and opponents are tested by the spectacle of believers who hold on. So the prayer in this verse is not a request for comfort; it is a request that the community’s endurance be allowed to testify, and that the testimony not be broken by collapse. The same concern shapes the Book’s account of earlier communities, who were afflicted with suffering and adversity until they asked when God’s help would come, and were answered that help is always near (2:214 — *“Indeed, Allah’s help is ˹always˺ near”*).

**The Forgiveness Sits in the Middle**

The prayer is built in three parts — protect us, forgive us, name Your power and wisdom — and the forgiveness in the middle carries its own argument. A community that begins by asking to be spared humiliation also admits that it has given its enemies material to work with. Sins weaken a people from the inside before any siege begins, and the Qur’an states the connection: “Indeed, Allah would never change a people’s state ˹of favour˺ until they change their own state ˹of faith˺.” (13:11). An earlier verse of the Book addresses the same logic from the other direction: Allah would never punish a people while His Prophet was among them, nor while they sought forgiveness (8:33 — *“But Allah would never punish them while you ˹O Prophet˺ were in their midst. Nor would He ever punish them if they prayed for forgiveness”*) — the presence of the righteous and the practice of asking are both shields. Taken together these verses explain the order of the petition here. Before asking that the enemy be checked, the community asks that its own record be cleared, because the wound that matters first is the one inside the camp.

The pairing runs through the Book as a signature ending: the same two names close the first verse of Sūrat al-Ṣaff, where all creation glorifies the One who is Mighty and Wise (61:1 — *“Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah. For He ˹alone˺ is the Almighty, All-Wise”*).

**Covered, Forgiven, and Protected**

Ibn Kathir explains *forgive us* in two parts: cover our faults so that no one but You sees them, and forgive what lies between us and You. The Arabic root of forgiveness, *gh-f-r*, first means to cover. The request is that the community’s mistakes not be shown to the enemy, which ties back to the first half of the prayer. A community whose faults are shown to the world becomes exactly the *fitnah* it has just asked God not to make it.

He glosses the two names that end the prayer in the same practical way. *Al-ʿAzīz*, the Almighty, means that those who seek refuge in God’s might are never wronged. *Al-Ḥakīm*, the All-Wise, means wise in His words, His actions, His laws and His decrees. The believers who have just lost their homes and their earthly protectors end the prayer by naming the two things they still have: a protector who cannot be defeated, and a plan that is never pointless.
verses.6:
> You certainly have an excellent example in them for whoever has hope in Allah and the Last Day. But whoever turns away, then surely Allah ˹alone˺ is the Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy

**An Example With a Condition Attached**

The model returns, and this time the verse states the price of admission: the example in Abraham and his companions is for whoever hopes in Allah and the Last Day. The qualification is not decorative. A community can admire a hero without following him, and admiration costs nothing while imitation costs a great deal — a house, a name in the family register, the protection of a clan. Hope in the meeting with God is the one motive strong enough to pay those costs, and the Book names it in the same terms elsewhere: “Whoever hopes for the meeting with Allah, ˹let them know that˺ Allah’s appointed time is sure to come.” (29:5).

**Hope as the Engine of Imitation**

The Arabic verb behind hope in this verse, *yarjū*, describes expectancy with desire — waiting for something good that one believes will come. The Book uses it as the motive for right action in several places: those who hope for the meeting with their Lord are told to do good deeds and not to associate anything with Him in worship (18:110 — *“So whoever hopes for the meeting with their Lord, let them do good deeds and associate none in the worship of their Lord.”*). The Prophet himself is given as an example for whoever has hope in Allah and the Last Day (33:21 — *“Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah you have an excellent example for whoever has hope in Allah and the Last Day, and remembers Allah often”*). The logic is economical and exact. Every departure made in the path of God involves giving up something that exists now for something that has been promised, and only hope can hold the two in view at the same time. The Emigrants of Madinah had left their houses, and Abraham had left his father’s household: the same transaction, differently charged. The verse therefore reduces the whole question of loyalty to a question about desire. Not what a man feels for his kin, but what he expects from his God, decides where his weight rests, and the Book states this as a law of human motivation rather than as a moral demand.

**Turning Away Harms No One Else**

The second half of the verse provides for the case of refusal, and it does so without the ordinary apparatus of threat: whoever turns away — then surely Allah is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy. The refuge of the Book here is not punishment but the independence of God, which is the most sobering thing that can be said to a person who imagines his obedience is needed. The same pair of names appears when earlier prophets made the same point to their own rebellious peoples. Moses said it to Israel: “If you along with everyone on earth were to be ungrateful, then ˹know that˺ Allah is indeed Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy.” (14:8). The sūrah of the Cave and the sūrah of Fāṭir say the same to humanity at large: “It is you who stand in need of Allah, but Allah ˹alone˺ is the Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy.” (35:15). The refusal contemplated in this verse is not a defeat for God. It is a self-inflicted loss, and the verse names the loss by naming the One who does not need the refuser.

The refusal is left standing as a possibility, and the community is not instructed to force the pattern on anyone: “Let there be no compulsion in religion, for the truth stands out clearly from falsehood.” (2:256).

**Rich Beyond Need, Praised in Every Act**

Ibn Kathir notes that this verse repeats the earlier statement about the excellent example, now with the exception already made. The repetition is for emphasis and encouragement: it presses the pattern of Abraham on everyone who believes in God and the return to Him. He explains *whoever turns away* as turning away from what God has commanded, and he joins the verse’s closing names to the verse where Moses tells his people that even if they and everyone on earth disbelieved, God would still be Self-Sufficient and Praiseworthy (14:8, quoted above).

On the names themselves, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that *al-Ghanī* is “the One who is perfectly rich”. Ibn Kathir adds that this is a quality only God can truly have, because He has no equal and nothing is like Him. *Al-Ḥamīd*, he says, is the One who is praised in all His words and actions. Put together, the names explain the tone of the whole verse. God is not hurt when someone refuses the example, because He needs nothing. And He is still praised when He lets the one who refuses go his own way, because even that choice falls within His wisdom.
verses.7:
> ˹In time,˺ Allah may bring about goodwill between you and those of them you ˹now˺ hold as enemies. For Allah is Most Capable. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**“It May Be” — a Door Left Open**

The verse turns on a single word: *ʿasā*, which expresses expectation rather than doubt. God may bring about goodwill between you and those of them you now hold as enemies. The construction is even more pointed in Arabic, since it sets God, the believers, and the hostile party inside one promise, with *mawadda*, warm affection, as the thing placed between them. The *mawadda* that the believers were forbidden to hand to the enemy in verse 1 becomes a gift God promises to create. The *ʿadāwa*, the enmity declared against idolaters in the story of Abraham, reappears in the participle *ʿādaytum*, "those you have made enemies." Nothing has been softened, and no command has been withdrawn.

**Capable of What Wealth Cannot Buy**

The middle of the verse states the reason for confidence: “For Allah is Most Capable.” The claim had already been showed in the same city, and the Book points to the proof. The tribes of Madinah, al-Aws and al-Khazraj, had been locked in a feud for generations that no mediator could settle; the Qur’an calls them out by name as the evidence: “He brought their hearts together. Indeed, He is Almighty, All-Wise.” (8:63).

Ibn Kathir describes the promised change in three pairs: affection after hostility, softness after hardness, and coming together after separation. He says God is able to bring opposites together and to join hearts after enmity and harshness. His witness is the Anṣār of Madinah. He quotes the verse that reminds them that they were enemies and God joined their hearts (3:103, quoted below), and the Prophet’s own words to them: “Did I not find you misguided, and God guided you through me? And divided, and God united you through me?” He also quotes the verse the section has already cited, that even if the Prophet had spent everything on earth he could not have united their hearts, but God united them (8:63, quoted above). The verse before it adds that God *supported* the Prophet *with His help and with the believers* (8:62 — *“He is the One Who has supported you with His help and with the believers”*). Joining the hearts of the believers is presented as part of that divine help. The same help is what this verse now offers the Emigrants and their relatives in Makkah.

**Forgiveness Aimed at Former Enemies**

The verse closes with two names that seem, at first glance, to belong to a different subject: Forgiving, Most Merciful. They are not an afterthought. The enmity contemplated here has a long history of injury, and the reconciliation being promised would be impossible if every act committed in the course of it remained chargeable. The Book applies the same logic to the men of Mecca who were taken captive at Badr: “If Allah finds goodness in your hearts, He will give you better than what has been taken from you, and forgive you.” (8:70). And at Ḥudaybiyyah, the Book reminds the believers of the restraint that had already been exercised on both sides: “He is the One Who held back their hands from you and your hands from them in the valley of ˹Ḥudaibiyah, near˺ Mecca, after giving you the upper hand over ˹a group of˺ them.” (48:24). The names Forgiving and Merciful at the end of this verse tell the injured party what the future of a successful reconciliation will require of them, and what God has already promised to supply.

Ibn Kathir reads the closing names as a promise aimed at the enemy as much as at the believers: God forgives the disbelief of disbelievers when they repent, return to their Lord and submit to Him in Islam, and He is Forgiving and Merciful to all who repent of any sin, whatever kind it is. That reading gives the verse a concrete future. The people the believers were told not to befriend in verse 1 are the same people God may forgive here. When much of Makkah entered Islam after the conquest, the promise of affection and the promise of forgiveness came true together.

**The Same Promise in Sūrat al-Rūm**

The Book states the promise of created affection as one of the signs by which God is known. “And one of His signs is that He created for you spouses from among yourselves so that you may find comfort in them. And He has placed between you compassion and mercy. Surely in this are signs for people who reflect.” (30:21). That verse speaks of marriage, and it uses the same word that appears here for the relationship of two nations — *mawadda*, with *raḥma* added to it, the very pair of attributes with which this verse ends. The community of Madinah had experienced both halves of the pattern. It had been a people of feuds who became brothers, and the Book makes that history the ground of its confidence: “Remember Allah’s favour upon you when you were enemies, then He united your hearts, so you—by His grace—became brothers.” (3:103). What had happened between tribes was possible between peoples.
verses.8:
> Allah does not forbid you from dealing kindly and fairly with those who have neither fought nor driven you out of your homes. Surely Allah loves those who are fair

**Asmāʾ’s Mother Comes to Madinah**

The occasion for the verse is recorded from Asmāʾ bint Abī Bakr, whose mother came to her in Madinah while still a polytheist, seeking some gift or favour from her daughter. Asmāʾ sent the question to the Prophet: my mother has come to me, wanting something from me — should I keep good relations with her? He answered: yes, keep good relations with her. The report is found in the two most reliable collections, and the verse was recognised as the ruling that answered her question (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2620; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1003). The detail that makes the report so instructive is that the woman was a polytheist of Mecca and the mother of a Muslim woman, and the answer was still toward kindness. Kindness to parents is not conditional on agreement in faith, and Islam did not dissolve the affections that God had placed in the family. Nor did the verse confine the concession to relatives: the words are general, so every Muslim may deal generously and fairly with any peaceful non-Muslim, and the closing sentence, that God loves those who are fair, applies to the dealings themselves.

**Qutaylah’s Gifts at the Door**

Ibn Kathir cites a second report, recorded by Imam Aḥmad from ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Zubayr, that adds details to Asmāʾ’s story. Her mother, Qutaylah, came to visit her with gifts: raisins, cheese and clarified butter. She was still an idolater at the time. At first Asmāʾ refused the gifts and would not let her into the house. ʿĀʾishah asked the Prophet about it, and God revealed this verse. The Prophet then told Asmāʾ to accept her mother’s gifts and let her in. The two reports together show both sides of the question. Asmāʾ’s first reaction came from loyalty to her faith. The verse told her that this loyalty did not require her to shut the door on a mother who had come in peace.

Ibn Kathir also names the kind of people the verse has in mind: disbelievers who did not fight the believers over religion and had no part in expelling them, such as women and those too weak to fight. Such people may be treated with *birr*, gentleness, and *qisṭ*, fairness. The ruling rests on what a person has done, not on the religion they follow.

**The Word Behind “Dealing Kindly”**

*Tabarrūhum* comes from the root that gives Arabic its word for filial duty, *birr*, the dutiful kindness a child owes a parent, and the verb carries the sense of treating someone generously, gently, and without ulterior motive. The Book uses the same moral vocabulary when it commands kindness to parents and uses it again when it commands the opposite of hostility. Alongside *birr* the verse places *iqsāṭ*, giving others their due and more precisely giving them the fair share of a thing, from the same root as *qisṭ*, the just balance. The pair is the most complete formula possible for ordinary coexistence: warmth in the treatment and fairness in the dealings. Both words are needed. Kindness without justice becomes partiality that wrongs a third party; justice without kindness becomes cold correctness, and the verse will not settle for either. “Indeed, Allah commands justice, grace, as well as courtesy to close relatives. He forbids indecency, wickedness, and aggression.” (16:90). The Book collapses the distance between the outer and the inner here: what is required of the believers is a settled posture toward people, not a permission slip for dislike. That God loves the fair is a statement worth pausing on, because it means fairness can be an act of worship by itself. The Book states the standard in the strongest terms for a community that had every reason to feel aggrieved: “O believers! Stand firm for Allah and bear true testimony. Do not let the hatred of a people lead you to injustice. Be just! That is closer to righteousness.” (5:8). Hatred is named as the thing most likely to make a believer wrong someone, and the Emigrants of Madinah had far more than a little hatred to manage.

**The Just on Platforms of Light**

On the verse’s last sentence, *Surely Allah loves those who are fair*, Ibn Kathir refers back to his commentary on Sūrat al-Ḥujurāt and repeats an authentic ḥadīth he had cited there: “The just will be on platforms of light at the right of the Throne. They are those who are fair in their judgements, with their families, and in whatever they are put in charge of.” The report shows how far fairness is meant to reach. It covers the courtroom, the household, and every position of responsibility. In this verse it also covers how a believer treats a peaceful neighbour of another faith. A Muslim who deals fairly with such a person is doing something God has promised to love and to honour on the Day of Judgement.

**When the Cause of the Boundary Ends**

The rule is phrased so that it dissolves when its cause dissolves. "Those who have neither fought nor driven you out" is the description of the people in question, and the shape of the sentence implies that their descendants or successors, who no longer do those things, are no longer addressed by the prohibition. The Book shows the same instinct in the verses that regulate war: “If the enemy is inclined toward peace, make peace with them. And put your trust in Allah.” (8:61). It goes further and prescribes the response that can end a feud permanently: “Good and evil cannot be equal. Respond ˹to evil˺ with what is best, then the one you are in a feud with will be like a close friend.” (41:34). So the boundary here is not a wall with a permanent tenant.
verses.9:
> Allah only forbids you from befriending those who have fought you for ˹your˺ faith, driven you out of your homes, or supported ˹others˺ in doing so. And whoever takes them as friends, then it is they who are the ˹true˺ wrongdoers

**Aiding the Wrongdoer Makes You a Partner**

The third clause rests on a principle that runs through the Book: sharing in an injustice is sharing the act. The verse names the expellers as the ones who *drove you out of your homes, or supported ˹others˺ in doing so*, and the phrasing places the supporter in the same sentence as the perpetrator. In another place the community is told plainly: “Cooperate with one another in goodness and righteousness, and do not cooperate in sin and transgression.” (5:2). The same logic appears in the law of war in the same sūrah’s wider context: those who “attacked you first” are the ones who must be answered (9:13 — *“Will you not fight those who have broken their oaths, conspired to expel the Messenger ˹from Mecca˺, and attacked you first?”*). A modern reader can see why the clause was necessary. Expulsion is rarely the work of an army alone; it is financed by merchants, blessed by poets, executed by mobs, and remembered by scribes. If the verse had named only those who carried the sword, the flatterers and financiers would have considered themselves outside the matter. The Qur’an refuses that division of labour, and it holds the whole apparatus of hostility responsible as a party.

**The Question the Verse Puts Back to the Reader**

The verse supplies its own diagnosis of how the fault works. Loyalty in these cases is not usually a decision arrived at openly; it is a slow transfer of trust, made in small payments, each one reasonable at the time. The Book answers this with a question aimed at the direction of the deal: “O believers! Do not take disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. Would you like to give Allah solid proof against yourselves?” (4:144). The image is legal and uncomfortable: the proof offered against the accused is his own record, handed in voluntarily. The verse under discussion states the same conclusion in a shorter form by naming the friend-taker himself as the wrongdoer, and it does not add a circumstance in which that verdict could be avoided. The only thing that changes it is a change in the other party’s conduct, which means the believer always has somewhere to look for hope and nothing to gain by pretending the evidence is unclear.

**The Verdict Matched in Sūrat al-Māʾidah**

Ibn Kathir explains the verse as forbidding friendship and alliance with disbelievers who are openly hostile: those who fought the believers, expelled them, and helped others expel them. With them, he says, God forbids friendship and requires the believers to treat them as enemies. He then notes that the verse’s last sentence, *whoever takes them as friends, then it is they who are the ˹true˺ wrongdoers*, strengthens the threat, and he links it to the verse in Sūrat al-Māʾidah that ends with the same verdict (5:51 — *“Whoever does so will be counted as one of them. Surely Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people”*). Both verses call the person who gives his loyalty to the enemy a wrongdoer. That is the word the Book uses for someone who puts a thing in the wrong place. Loyalty that belongs to God and the believers, handed to people at war with them, is loyalty in the wrong place.

Ibn Kathir treats verses 8 and 9 as one pair: kindness is allowed toward those who do not fight, and friendship is forbidden with those who do. The sūrah itself makes the second rule depend on the three acts it lists, so the prohibition does not stretch beyond them. This fits what verse 8 settled: the boundary is set by conduct, and it moves when the conduct changes.
verses.10:
> O believers! When the believing women come to you as emigrants, test their intentions—their faith is best known to Allah—and if you find them to be believers, then do not send them back to the disbelievers. These ˹women˺ are not lawful ˹wives˺ for the disbelievers, nor are the disbelievers lawful ˹husbands˺ for them. ˹But˺ repay the disbelievers whatever ˹dowries˺ they had paid. And there is no blame on you if you marry these ˹women˺ as long as you pay them their dowries. And do not hold on to marriage with polytheistic women. ˹But˺ demand ˹repayment of˺ whatever ˹dowries˺ you had paid, and let the disbelievers do the same. That is the judgment of Allah—He judges between you. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise

**“Test Them” — the Sūrah’s Name Comes From Here**

*Famtaḥinūhunna* — examine them, put them to the test — comes from a root used for assaying metal to separate the pure from the alloy, and the sūrah takes its name, al-Mumtaḥanah, from this command. The examination was practical, not mystical. A woman might have left Mecca because she believed, or because a husband ill-treated her, or because she followed a man to Madinah; the community was told to establish her intention before acting, since the ruling that follows depended completely on her being a believer. The same verse immediately sets a limit on human testing, and the limit is the mercy in it: “their faith is best known to Allah.” (60:10) The community judges what it can see, and God holds the secret of the heart. This division of labour protects both sides. The woman is not asked to prove her conscience beyond a honest account of it, and the community is not permitted to keep interrogating what only God can inspect.

**How the Women Were Examined**

The early commentators explain what *test their intentions* meant in practice. Al-ʿAwfī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās: “Their test was to ask them to bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is His servant and Messenger.” Mujāhid described the questioning in more detail: “Ask them why they came. If they came because they were angry with their husbands, or for some other reason, and you find that they have not believed, send them back to their husbands.” Ibn Kathir draws a doctrinal point from the next clause, *if you find them to be believers*: it shows that faith can be known and confirmed from what a person says and shows, even though the verse has just said that God knows it best. The community acts on the evidence it can see and leaves what is hidden to God.

**Why She Could Not Be Sent Back**

The prohibition is stated with the symmetry of a legal rule: these women are not lawful wives for the disbelievers, nor are the disbelievers lawful husbands for them. That sentence does the work of the whole passage. Returning the woman would hand her back into a marriage that the revelation no longer recognised, and would make the Muslim community an enforcer of a contract it deemed void. The Qur’an had already established the principle in an earlier sūrah, where marriage to idolaters is forbidden in both directions: “Do not marry polytheistic women until they believe… And do not marry polytheistic men until they believe” (2:221, in meaning). The treaty with Quraysh could not override a religious prohibition, and the community could not lawfully deliver a believing woman into the authority of a man whose religion she had left. What looked like a violation of the agreement was, in the commentators’ explanation, the removal of a party from the agreement’s scope: the clause had been designed with runaway men in view, and its plain sense could not be stretched to cover this.

The arrangement was humiliating in appearance and was accepted because the Book calls the treaty itself a clear victory (48:1 — *“Indeed, We have granted you a clear triumph ˹O Prophet˺”*).

**The Treaty Clause and What the Verse Did to It**

Ibn Kathir begins with the text of the treaty of Ḥudaybiyyah as the early authorities reported it: “Every man”, and in another wording “every person”, “who comes from us to you is to be returned to us, even if he follows your religion.” He names ʿUrwah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd, al-Zuhrī, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān and al-Suddī as reporting this. On the first wording, the verse specifies and explains what the agreement meant, and Ibn Kathir calls this “the best way of understanding it”. Some of the early generations held instead that the verse cancelled that part of the treaty. Both views reach the same practical result: believing women were not returned.

He also cites a report from ʿAbdullāh ibn Abī Aḥmad ibn Jaḥsh that names the people involved. Umm Kulthūm bint ʿUqbah ibn Abī Muʿayṭ emigrated, and her brothers ʿUmārah and al-Walīd followed her to Madinah. They spoke to the Prophet and asked for her to be returned. God then removed the women from the treaty in particular, forbade returning Muslim women to the idolaters, and revealed the verse about testing them. The report of al-Miswar and Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam in the Ṣaḥīḥ gives the same setting: after the treaty was made, believing women came to the Prophet, and this passage was revealed about them.

**Zaynab and Abū al-ʿĀṣ**

Ibn Kathir notes that *These ˹women˺ are not lawful ˹wives˺ for the disbelievers* ended an arrangement that had been allowed in the early years of Islam, when a Muslim woman could remain married to an idolater. The best-known case is the Prophet’s own daughter. Zaynab was married to Abū al-ʿĀṣ ibn al-Rabīʿ, who stayed an idolater like his people. He was captured at Badr, and Zaynab sent a necklace to pay his ransom. It had belonged to her mother, Khadījah. When the Prophet saw it he was deeply moved and said to his Companions, “If you see fit to free her prisoner for her, then do so.” They did. As part of the arrangement, Abū al-ʿĀṣ was to send Zaynab to her father, and he kept his word, sending her to Madinah with Zayd ibn Ḥārithah. She stayed in Madinah from the year of Badr, the second year after the Hijrah, until her husband became Muslim in the eighth year. She then went back to him under their first marriage, without a new dowry.

**ʿUmar Lets Two Marriages Go**

The clause *do not hold on to marriage with polytheistic women* applied the same rule to Muslim men, and Ibn Kathir explains it as forbidding believers either to marry idolatrous women or to stay married to them. The report of al-Miswar and Marwān records how quickly it was obeyed. After the passage was revealed, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb divorced two wives who were still idolaters. One later married Muʿāwiyah ibn Abī Sufyān, and the other married Ṣafwān ibn Umayyah. ʿUmar was the man who had asked to strike Ḥāṭib’s neck in the first episode of the sūrah. Here he applies the sūrah’s law to his own household without delay.

Ibn Kathir also explains the money clauses. *Repay the disbelievers whatever they had paid* means returning to the idolater husbands the dowries they had given the emigrant women. He says this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah, al-Zuhrī and others. *No blame on you if you marry these women as long as you pay them their dowries* is explained with its conditions: the woman’s waiting period must be over, and the marriage must be concluded properly, with a guardian and the other requirements. Al-Zuhrī, in the report of Maʿmar, sums up the whole arrangement: the verse came while the Prophet was at Ḥudaybiyyah after the peace. Dowries paid for the women who came were to be returned to their husbands, and in the same way the idolaters were to return the dowries of any Muslim wives who went over to them. *That is the judgment of Allah*, Ibn Kathir says, refers to this ruling about the treaty and the removal of women from its terms.

**What the Verse Commanded After the Test**

The rest of the verse handles the money and the marriages. Since the women were believers and their former husbands were not, the verse states that neither is lawful for the other, and then gives the practical rule: give the women what they have spent, meaning their dowries where they are due, and there is no blame on the believers in marrying them once their waiting period is over and their dowries are paid. It then turns to the women who stayed behind with disbelieving husbands, and it tells the believers to ask for what was spent on them, just as the disbelievers may ask for whatever they spent on the women who left. The sentence closes by saying that this is God's judgement, and that He is knowing and wise.

**The Ruling Built Into the Passage**

The passage made faith the basis of the marriage bond. A woman who left Makkah because she believed could not be sent back to a husband who did not share that faith, and the community was not allowed to keep her dowry or her household. The sūrah then states the reciprocal duty two verses later, where if any of the wives of the Muslims go over to the disbelievers, the community is to pay the men what they spent from the funds available (60:11 — *“And if any of your wives desert you to the disbelievers, and later you take spoils from them, then pay those whose wives have gone, the equivalent of whatever ˹dowry˺ they had paid.”*). The rule is symmetrical for a reason: the new community was building a law of marriage that could not be accused of taking what belonged to others.

**Why This Needed to Be Said in This Sūrah**

The sūrah was given after the treaty of Ḥudaybiyyah, when the emigration of the women to Madinah became a political problem between the two cities. The report of the occasion names Umm Kulthūm bint ʿUqbah as one of the women who came, and the families left behind demanded their return under the terms of the treaty. The verse tells the Prophet what to do with the treaty's terms: the believers were not to return the believing women, because the treaty covered people, not faith. The Book, in short, draws the line between a written agreement and a creed, and it does so while keeping the money accounted for on both sides.
verses.11:
> And if any of your wives desert you to the disbelievers, and later you take spoils from them, then pay those whose wives have gone, the equivalent of whatever ˹dowry˺ they had paid. And be mindful of Allah, in Whom you believe

**The Other Half of the Arrangement**

The previous verse dealt with women arriving in Madinah and the men they left in Mecca. This verse handles the reverse traffic: Muslim wives who go over to the disbelievers, and the men they leave behind, whose dowers went with them. The problem was real on both sides of the line, and the Book refuses to legislate for only the side it favours. The instruction here is that when a Muslim has lost a wife to the enemy camp, he receives the equivalent of what he had spent on her. That is the plain reading of *fa-ātū lladhīna dhahabat azwājuhum mithla mā anfaqū* — give those whose wives have gone the like of what they spent. The verse names the loss as financial before it is emotional, and it treats the money as a recoverable claim rather than as a casualty of war. Anyone who has watched a conflict narrated by only one side can see the originality in that. The revelation is careful that its own community does not become the party that keeps two sets of books.

**When the Other Side Refused to Pay**

The early commentators explain what situation this verse was meant for. Mujāhid and Qatādah said it concerns disbelievers who had no peace treaty with the Muslims: if a Muslim’s wife fled to them and they did not pay back what her husband had spent on her, then when a woman came from their side to the Muslims, nothing was to be returned to her husband until the Muslim who lost his wife had been paid the like of what he had spent.

Ibn Jarīr recorded a fuller account from al-Zuhrī. The believers accepted God’s ruling and paid the idolaters what they owed for the dowries of the women who had emigrated. The idolaters refused to accept the ruling and would not pay what they owed the Muslims. So God revealed this verse. From then on, if a Muslim woman went over to the idolaters, the believers were to repay her Muslim husband his dowry out of whatever money they still held from the dowries of emigrant women, money that would otherwise have gone back to the idolater husbands. Anything left over after that was still to be returned to them. This is why the verse speaks of *taking spoils* or “getting the upper hand”. The loss is made good from what the other side has forfeited, and the Muslims do not keep more than the debt. The closing call to *be mindful of Allah* guards the arithmetic. Even when the other party had broken faith, the believers were to take back what was owed and no more.

**Be Mindful of God, in Whom You Believe**

The verse ends without a threat and without a promise of reward: “And be mindful of Allah, in Whom you believe.” (60:11) The clause at the end is unusual. Ordinarily the Book calls people to mindfulness before stating what is required; here it asks for mindfulness after telling them to part with money they had lost, and it grounds the appeal in the belief the listeners already have — you believe in Him, so act as those who do. It is the most persuasive form of argument the Book uses with its own community, because it puts the obligation where the listener’s own commitments already are. A man who has accepted that God is the provider of all that he owns has small reason to object when a command asks him to hand over a portion of it. A man who believes in the judgement of God has every reason to keep his accounts straight even when no human court will make him.
verses.12:
> O Prophet! When the believing women come to you, pledging to you that they will neither associate anything with Allah ˹in worship˺, nor steal, nor fornicate, nor kill their children, nor falsely attribute ˹illegitimate˺ children to their husbands, nor disobey you in what is right, then accept their pledge, and ask Allah to forgive them. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**A Pledge Taken Directly From Women**

*Bayʿah* is a covenant of allegiance, the same word used for the oath of the men of Madinah and for the pledge under the tree at Ḥudaybiyyah, and this verse applies it to women arriving in Madinah on their own. ʿĀʾishah described how the Prophet administered it: he would recite this verse and accept the pledge from women by words alone, and his hand never touched a woman’s hand (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 7214). The manner of taking the pledge carries as much instruction as the pledge itself, since the community was watching and the convention of a spoken oath, administered publicly and without contact, showed that the covenant with women was a religious act rather than a private arrangement. Nothing in the verse requires a husband, a guardian, or a male sponsor to bring the woman to the Prophet. She comes, she pledges, and she is regarded. That independence is not incidental to the passage; the sūrah has been legislating for women who were separated from their men by the decision of conscience, and it presumes throughout that a woman’s faith is her own affair.

**“As Far as You Are Able”**

Ibn Kathir records how the verse was used at the time. ʿĀʾishah said that the Prophet used to examine the women who emigrated to him by this verse, reciting it to them. When a woman accepted its conditions, he would say, “I have accepted your pledge.” It was spoken only. She swore that his hand never touched a woman’s hand during the pledge. Imam Aḥmad recorded the account of Umaymah bint Ruqayqah, who came with a group of women to pledge. The Prophet took from them the pledge that is in the Qurʾān, and then added, “As far as you are able and can bear.” The women said, “Allah and His Messenger are more merciful to us than we are to ourselves.” They asked whether he would shake hands with them. He said, “I do not shake hands with women. My word to one woman is like my word to a hundred.” Ibn Kathir says this ḥadīth has a sound chain, and that al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah also collected it. The words “as far as you are able” show the spirit of the pledge. It was a serious covenant, but it was given by people who would still be judged by what they were able to do.

Imam Aḥmad also recorded from ʿĀʾishah that Fāṭimah bint ʿUtbah came to pledge, and when the Prophet recited *that they will not associate anything with Allah, nor steal, nor fornicate*, she put her hand on her head out of shyness. The Prophet approved of her modesty. ʿĀʾishah said to her, “Go on and pledge, woman. By Allah, we all pledged to the very same.” She agreed and gave her pledge on the terms of the verse.

**Theft, and Hind’s Question**

Ibn Kathir explains *nor steal* as taking other people’s property, and then gives an important limit to it. A wife whose husband does not provide for her may take a reasonable amount from his wealth to cover her needs, whether he knows or not. His evidence is the case of Hind bint ʿUtbah, recorded in both Ṣaḥīḥs. She said, “O Messenger of Allah, Abū Sufyān is a stingy man. He does not give me enough for myself and my children. May I take from his money without his knowledge?” The Prophet said, “Take from his wealth, in the right way, what is enough for you and your children.” The pledge forbids theft, but the Prophet did not treat a wife taking what she is already owed as theft.

**The Practice the Pledge Ended**

Fourth in the list stands the killing of children, and the Book elsewhere names what was being forbidden. The Qur’an describes the pre-Islamic Arab father given news of a daughter: his face darkens… and he hides from the people because of the bad news, asking himself whether to keep her in disgrace or bury her alive; then it pronounces its judgement on that reasoning, “Evil indeed is their judgment!” (16:58–59). Sūrat al-Takwīr makes the buried girl a witness at the resurrection: “and when baby girls, buried alive, are asked for what crime they were put to death” (81:8–9). The pledge therefore abolished by covenant what the community had practised by custom, and it did so by putting the practice among the sins that bar entry to the faith rather than among the errors that a convert might mend at leisure. The verse also shows the moral reach of the pledge. It is not a document about worship alone. It binds the woman to protect the very lives that her society had taught her were expendable, and it makes that protection part of her covenant with God and His Prophet.

On *nor fornicate*, Ibn Kathir points to the general command in the Book (17:32 — *“Do not go near adultery. It is truly a shameful deed and an evil way”*) and mentions a ḥadīth from Samurah describing a painful punishment in the Fire for those who commit it. On *nor kill their children*, he says the clause covers killing children after birth, which the people of the Jāhiliyyah did out of fear of poverty (6:151 — *“Do not kill your children for fear of poverty. We provide for you and for them.”*). He also says it covers killing a child in the womb, which some ignorant women did for bad reasons.

**A Slander Between Hands and Feet**

The Arabic behind *nor falsely attribute ˹illegitimate˺ children to their husbands* speaks literally of “a slander they invent between their hands and their feet”, and the translation’s wording follows the early explanation. Ibn ʿAbbās said it means that a woman must not attribute to her husband a child who is not his, and Muqātil said the same. The image points to the body, to the child carried and born, and it names the most private kind of deception. The lie wrongs the husband, and it also passes false lineage and inheritance on to others.

**Obedience Only in What Is Right**

Ibn Kathir explains *nor disobey you in what is right* as obeying the Prophet when he commands good and forbids evil. Al-Bukhārī recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās that this was “one of the conditions that Allah laid down for the women”. Maymūn ibn Mihrān drew a lesson from the wording: “Allah did not command obedience even to His Prophet except in what is right, and what is right is itself obedience.” Ibn Zayd made the same point: God ordered that His Messenger, the best of His creation, be obeyed in what is right. If even the Prophet’s authority is described with this limit, no lesser authority can demand more.

The women themselves understood part of *what is right* in terms of mourning. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded from Umm ʿAṭiyyah that when the Prophet took their pledge and recited *that they will not associate anything with Allah*, he also forbade them to wail over the dead. One woman pulled back her hand and said, “A certain woman helped me wail for one of my relatives, and I must repay her.” The Prophet said nothing against it. She went, returned, and gave her pledge. In the version Ibn Jarīr recorded, Umm ʿAṭiyyah added that only this woman and Umm Sulaym bint Milḥān, the mother of Anas ibn Mālik, did so. Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded from one of the women who pledged: “Part of the good in which we promised not to disobey him was that we would not scratch our faces, tear out our hair, rip our clothes, or wail.” The pledge reached into the customs of grief, and the women took it seriously enough to settle an old debt before they gave it.

**The Same Pledge Taken From Men**

The terms of this verse were not only for women.
