Imam Aḥmad recorded from ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit that the Prophet said to the men sitting with him, “Pledge to me that you will not associate anything with Allah, nor steal, nor commit adultery, nor kill your children.” He recited the verse about the believing women, took the pledge on it, and then said: “Whoever among you keeps it, his reward is with Allah. Whoever falls into any of it and is punished for it, the punishment is an expiation for him. And whoever falls into any of it and Allah covers it for him, his case is with Allah: if He wills He forgives him, and if He wills He punishes him.” Ibn Kathir notes that both Ṣaḥīḥs contain the report. It shows that the women’s pledge became the model for the community as a whole, and the closing words match the verse’s own ending: *ask Allah to forgive them. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful*.

**Their Own Standing Before God**

Because the pledge was taken from women directly, the verse establishes in the plainest way that women are religiously independent persons. The Qur’an elsewhere lists the qualities of believing men and believing women in matching pairs and assigns them a single outcome: “Surely ˹for˺ Muslim men and women, believing men and women, devout men and women, truthful men and women, patient men and women, humble men and women, charitable men and women, fasting men and women, men and women who guard their chastity. Men and women who remember Allah often—for ˹all of˺ them Allah has prepared forgiveness and a great reward.” (33:35).
verses.13:
> O believers! Do not ally yourselves with a people Allah is displeased with. They already have no hope for the Hereafter, just like the disbelievers lying in ˹their˺ graves

**A Line Drawn at the End of the Sūrah**

The verse forbids the believers to take as allies a people whom God has been angry with, and it closes the sūrah on the same note it opened on. The first verse of the sūrah forbids taking the enemies of God and the enemies of the believers as friends and offering them loyalty while they have rejected the truth that has come (60:1 states the prohibition — *“O believers! Do not take My enemies and yours as trusted allies, showing them affection even though they deny what has come to you of the truth.”*), and this last verse returns to the same instruction with the same seriousness.

**What the Phrase Means**

The people described as under God's anger have despaired of the world to come, and the verse compares them to those who reject the faith despairing over the companions of the graves. The commentators read the closing image in two ways. Some said the disbelievers have no hope for the dead at all, since they do not believe in a resurrection, so a grave ends everything for them. Others said the image is set against what a believer holds: he stands at a grave with hope for what comes after it, and the difference between the two outlooks is the difference between two ways of living.

Ibn Kathir explains the closing image in two ways. In the first, the disbelievers have given up hope of ever meeting their buried relatives again, because they do not believe in the resurrection. In the second, the image describes the disbelievers who are already in their graves. They have lost all hope of any good once they have seen the punishment and learned that the resurrection is real. Al-Aʿmash reported, through Abū al-Ḍuḥā and Masrūq, that Ibn Masʿūd explained the phrase this way: “Just as the disbeliever despairs when he dies and sees and knows what his reward will be.” Ibn Kathir says this is also the view of Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Muqātil, Ibn Zayd, al-Kalbī and Manṣūr, and that Ibn Jarīr preferred it. On this reading, the people God is displeased with have, in this life, already reached the hopelessness the disbelieving dead reach at the grave.

**Who the Commentators Meant**

The occasions reported for the verse concern poor Muslims in Madinah who were selling information about the community's movements to the Jews of the city in exchange for provisions. The commentators differ over the reference of the phrase, and each reading has its grounds. Some identified the people as the Jews of Madinah, whose opposition to the Prophet had brought them under judgement. Some saw the hypocrites, who concealed their cooperation with the community's enemies. Others read the words as a general description of everyone who has earned God's anger by choosing the world over the last life.

The readings do not contradict each other so much as weight the verse differently, and the general reading has the strongest claim to be its purpose, since a rule that applied only to a group that has vanished would be a report rather than a command.

Ibn Kathir takes the phrase *a people Allah is displeased with* broadly: the Jews, the Christians and the rest of the disbelievers who earned God’s anger and were rejected by Him. He puts God’s question to the believers this way: how can you make them your allies, friends and companions after God has decided that they have no hope of any good in the Hereafter? He also notes the structure of the sūrah, which ends with the same prohibition it began with. As the sūrah itself has taught, the prohibition applies to alliance with those who fight the faith, not to the fair and kind dealing that verse 8 allows.

**The Criterion the Verse Fixes**

What the verse settles is the test. It is not this tribe or that community. It is the condition of having given up on the life to come. Anyone in that condition stands on the wrong side of the line, whichever city he lives in and whichever community he belongs to.

That is why the sūrah closes with this verse rather than with a list of names. The reader is being given a way to judge a friendship by what the friend expects from the future, and by where his hope is placed when the grave comes up in conversation. The sūrah has spent its verses distinguishing loyalty to God from loyalty to people who fight Him, and it ends by naming the spiritual condition that produces the second kind of loyalty.

**What the Rest of the Sūrah Said About Fairness**

The sūrah kept the door of kindness open while it drew this line. It says that God does not forbid the believers from being kind and just to those who did not fight them and did not drive them out of their homes, and it forbids only the alliance with those who fought them and drove them out and helped to expel them (60:8 — *“Allah does not forbid you from dealing kindly and fairly with those who have neither fought nor driven you out of your homes. Surely Allah loves those who are fair”* and 60:9 — *“Allah only forbids you from befriending those who have fought you for ˹your˺ faith, driven you out of your homes, or supported ˹others˺ in doing so.”* give the two rulings). So the last verse is not a licence for hostility toward people of other faiths. It is a rule about a specific relationship, the one in which a believer hands his safety and his loyalty to people who are working against the faith, and the Book treats that as the one friendship a believer cannot keep.
